Honestly, I have to say YTA (you're the asshole) for not cutting the customer's hair in this situation. I get that your shop follows a women-by-appointment policy, and that the policy is posted clearly on your signage, Facebook, and website. I understand, too, that most of your staff are Muslim, and it’s a big religious boundary for male employees not to touch women's hair unless they're family. Plus, you haven’t trained your male staff in cutting women’s hair, partly because of religious practice, partly because it requires different techniques and tools.

But in this case, it sounds like a male-passing woman came in requesting a straightforward men’s haircut. The price would have been the same, but instead, you told this customer they had to make an appointment so the female stylist—who only comes in at certain times—could serve her, despite the customer seeming to just want a regular men’s cut.

I understand wanting to respect your staff and your posted policies, but you run a barbershop that's 99% men and you do sometimes serve women. Turning away someone based on their *perceived* gender (or gender presentation) instead of the specific service request feels unfair and exclusionary. The fact that your staff’s discomfort comes from only serving women via appointments because of religious concerns makes this really complicated—but at the end of the day, if your business is publicly open for walk-in men’s haircuts, and someone comes in solo, presenting male and requesting a “men’s” style, what’s the harm? Especially since the price and style are the same, and this customer clearly expected equal service.

In my opinion, this kind of rigid rule, especially when strictly enforced based on your assumptions about someone’s sex/gender, crosses into discrimination. I get you felt bad, but in this case, the right thing would have been to serve the customer or at very least, be more flexible if your mission is genuinely about hair and not about exclusion.

Bottom line: rules that result in unfair treatment need to be reconsidered, even if your intentions weren’t malicious. If your shop is open for men’s cuts without an appointment, the same service should be available to anyone asking for it, regardless of gender identity. Sorry, but YTA here.

Honestly, in this situation, I do think you were in the wrong ("yes" to being the asshole). Here’s why:

I understand that your shop has a women-by-appointment policy, which is posted clearly on your signage, Facebook, and website. The fact that your staff are primarily Muslim and male staff follow a religious rule about not touching women’s hair makes sense, and I respect your need to abide by your values.

Plus, you point out that your staff aren’t trained in women’s haircuts—citing differences in religious practice, technique, and the products/tools you use. That explanation, along with the need to give a couple hours’ notice to bring in your female stylist, shows you do have a process in place for female clients. The price would have been the same, so it’s not about overcharging either.

However, for me, the problem is how rigidly your staff stuck to those policies in a way that really hurt someone, especially someone who, according to your manager, was a male-passing woman wanting a men’s style haircut. When someone presents and identifies in a particular way and requests a common men’s style you *are* equipped to provide, I think you should err on the side of inclusivity, or at least try to handle it with as much care and understanding as possible.

Even with a clear policy, turning the customer away on the spot—when your shop literally cuts this style of hair daily—comes across as exclusionary, even if unintentional. It also sounds like the staff gave little effort explaining the system compassionately or offering alternatives, which can feel careless and dismissive.

I get that following religious beliefs is important, but there has to be a way to balance that with treating every customer with respect, urgency, and avoided embarrassment, especially in 2024 when we’re trying to be more accommodating of gender diversity. If your staff doesn’t feel equipped for these edge cases, maybe it’s time to revisit your training, front-door explanations, or the flexibility of your scheduling. No one should leave a business feeling judged or unwelcome, regardless of gender or appearance.

Bottom line: Your shop could’ve handled this much better and made the customer feel less singled out. So yes, you were the asshole here.
